en: The Means for the Sadhana of Hevajra.
Homage to the glorious Hevajra!
Having paid homage with devotion to the glorious Hevajra and also to Nairātmyā, [I shall compose this work].
I shall explain the method for accomplishing that through the grace of the Vajrācārya.

First, the yogin—having propitiated a true guru who is intent on the welfare of all sentient beings; having been consecrated according to the ritual procedure by means of the mandala installation as taught in the *Śrī Hevajra*; having received full authorization; having attained the perfectly pure knowledge of reality free from error; and having obtained the [auspicious] signs—desiring to accomplish the glorious *Hevajra*, should dwell in a delightful place such as a cremation ground. Accompanied by his consort (*vidyā*) and partaking of the pledges (*samaya*) such as the five nectars, he should perform the offerings of bali and worship. Then, he should visualize a blue syllable *HŪṂ* arising from a sun disk produced from the letter *Repha* in his own heart. From that *HŪṂ*, he should emanate rays of light in five forms into the expanse of the sky, and by those rays, he should draw forth before him in the space of the sky the Blessed One, Vajra-born, blue in color, with the faces, arms, and weapons to be described hereafter—whether sixteen-armed, six-armed, four-armed, or two-armed—embraced by his consort, three-eyed, with yellow hair standing upright, endowed with the six mudrās, surrounded by eight goddesses, and whose form consists of the process of radiating and reabsorbing. He should meditate upon him thus.

In front of him is Gaurī, dark blue in color, holding the moon of bodhicitta in her hand; to the south is Caurī, yellow, holding a self-arisen flower (svayambhūkusuma) in the hand of the sun; behind him is Vetālī, red, holding a vajra-water vessel in her hand; to the north is Ghasmarī, dark green, holding secret medicine; in the northeast is Pukkasī, blue, holding various kinds of meat; in the southeast is Śabarī, white, holding a vessel of liquid (rasa) in her hand; in the southwest is Caṇḍālī, slightly red, playing a kṛpīṭa drum; and in the northwest is Ḍombinī, smoke-colored, embracing her own body.

Having thus beheld the Blessed Lord, the Bhaṭṭāraka, in the sky, whose form consists of the emanation and reabsorption [of light], one should worship him with the specific outer and secret reality-offerings (tattvapūjā) emerging from the seed-syllable situated in one’s own heart. Then, in his presence, one should perform the rites beginning with the confession of misdeeds (*pāpadeśanā*). Whatever evil karma has been committed by me throughout the beginningless course of *saṃsāra*, born of unreal conceptual constructions—all that I confess before the Blessed One so that it shall not be done again. I rejoice in all the merit of all sentient beings and dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). All this, consisting of the three realms...

Having taken refuge in the Buddha as the He-ka-ra-vajra in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), in the Dharma which is the nature of the mantras, mudrās, maṇḍalas, and so forth taught by him, and in the assembly of deities situated within that previous wheel, one should cultivate great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*)—characterized by the love for an only son toward all sentient beings who are of the nature of fire—and the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) characterized by emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects, which serves as the cause for accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings.

Thereafter, having seen sentient beings submerged in the ocean of conceptual construction and without refuge, and having brought to manifestation great compassion whose very nature is the desire to deliver them, the practitioner—having attained such great joy, being equanimous toward all imagined objects, and desiring to grasp the essence of the reality of all things without exception—should recite the mantra: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness. Immediately following this, while bringing the meaning of the mantra to manifestation, he should cause himself and the entire triple world to become non-apparent (*nirābhāsa*). Then, recollecting his vow (*praṇidhāna*), he should visualize in space a solar disc arising from the syllable *repha* (Ṛ). In its center, he should see a double-pronged universal vajra (*viśvavajra*) with five rays of light, produced from the syllable *hūṃ*. From its rays, he should perceive a blazing vajra-fence (*vajraprākāra*) extending as far as desired. Having visualized a vajra-canopy (*vajrapañjara*) within that, he should dispel obstructors and meditate on Wisdom (*prajñā*) pervading the space in the middle, in the form of a white letter *E*. Above that, he should visualize the earth, square and green, born from the syllable *laṃ*. Then, the circular water-maṇḍala, white and born from the syllable *vaṃ*. Then, the triangular fire-maṇḍala, red and born from the syllable *raṃ*. Then, the wind-maṇḍala, half-moon shaped and blue in color, born from the syllable *yaṃ*.
Having recognized the consciousness situated within that [space] and having transformed all this, one should instantly meditate upon the mandala in the form of a wheel, luminous.

One should clearly visualize a square [mandala] with four gates, adorned with eight pillars, and embellished with hanging necklaces (*hāra*), half-necklaces (*arddhahāra*), arches (*toraṇa*), and so forth. In its center, within the union of the moon and sun, are a skull-cup and a flaying knife produced from the two seed-syllables *hūṃ* and *aṃ*; above those are the same two seed-syllables. One should perceive oneself as the complete transformation of all these, in the form of the illustrious Hevajra: blue in color, with eight faces, sixteen arms, and four legs, engaged in the blissful union of the couple Nairātmyā and himself, characterized by the supreme joy and great bliss of their mutual delight. Then: *Oṃ, O noble bliss of the lotus, giver of the bliss of great passion, partaker of the four joys, O Universal One (*viśva*), *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, perform my task! Oṃ, O Great Hatred of the Vajra, giver of the four joys, O Lord whose mouth is the sky (*khagamukha*) and who is of one flavor, *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, perform my task!*

Even in the external ritual for generating bliss, this consecration of the lotus and vajra must be performed. Then, through the union of the churner and the churned, one should emanate the circle of deities. Therein, in the eastern and other doors, one should visualize Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Rudra in due order; likewise, in the corners beginning with the northeast, Vaivasvata and Vittanāyaka, and in the southwest, Vemacitrin. Having thus visualized the eight seats, one should perceive the eight seed-syllables—*gaṃ caṃ vaṃ ghaṃ paṃ śaṃ laṃ ḍaṃ*—within the midst of the joined moon and sun disks upon them.

The symbols of Gaurī and the others are the transformations of those [seeds]. One should visualize a knife, a fire-pit, a tortoise, a serpent, a lion, a mendicant’s staff, a wheel, and a vajra; above those, once again, those very same seed-syllables. Having transformed everything into one, one should meditate on the perfected forms of Gaurī and the others.

There, at the eastern gate, one should visualize Gaurī, born from the syllable *gaṃ*, black in color, holding a flaying knife in her right hand and a red lotus in her left; she stands upon Brahmā and has the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). At the southern gate, one should visualize Caurī, born from the syllable *caṃ*, of a madder-red hue, holding a sacrificial ladle (*kṛpīṭa*) in her right hand and a boar in her left; she is mounted upon Indra and is the very essence of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*). At the western gate, one should contemplate Vetālī, born from the syllable *vaṃ*, with the luster of molten gold, holding a tortoise in her right arm and a lotus vessel in her left; she stands upon Upendra and is fashioned from the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*). At the northern gate, one should visualize Ghasmarī, produced from the syllable *ghaṃ*, dark green in color, holding a snake in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left; she is mounted upon Rudra and has the nature of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). In the northeast corner, [one should visualize] Pukkasī, born from the syllable *puṃ*.

One should visualize [the goddess] of blue complexion, holding a lion in her right hand and an axe in her left, treading upon Vaivasvata (Yama), and having the nature of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). In the southeast corner, one should see Śabarī, born from the syllable *Śaṃ*, white in color, holding a mendicant bowl (*bhikṣu*) in her right hand and a *khiṅkhirikā* (a small vessel) in her left, mounted upon Vittanāyaka (Kubera), and having the nature of the water element (*ab-dhātu*). In the southwest corner, one should see Caṇḍālī, born from the syllable *Laṃ*, resembling the sky, holding a discus in her right hand and a plow in her left, treading upon a Rākṣasa, and having the nature of the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*). In the northwest corner, one should meditate on Ḍombinī, born from the syllable *Ḍaṃ*, of variegated color, holding a vajra in her right hand and a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) in her left, mounted upon Vemacitrin, and having the nature of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). All of these should be visualized as three-eyed, with faces terrifying with fangs, with tawny hair standing erect, naked, adorned with the five mudrās, standing in the dancing posture of half-lotus (*ardhaparyaṅka*), arisen from the emission of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Immediately thereafter, the Blessed One, having melted away through his union with his own consort (*svavidyā*)—who is of the single flavor of the most intense and supreme great bliss—remained in the form of his seed-syllable. Then, the four goddesses, Pukkasī and the others, thinking "We are without a protector," fell into great despondency.
Being exceedingly longing, they rouse the Blessed One with vajra-songs that awaken the mind:
"Arise, O Lord! O essence of compassion! Protect me, Pukkasī!"
O Mahāsua, having abandoned the intoxication of desire, I have attained the samādhi of emptiness.
Even though I am thus distressed, I die; arise, O Hevajra!
Abandon this nature of emptiness, O Śavarī; let the work of the lioness be done.
O Lord of the Gods, hear my request: why do you remain in solitude?
I am a Caṇḍālī; I entreat you, yet though entreated by me, you are not seen.
O Indīālī, arise! I know your heart;
O Dombī, you who are the essence of skill, do not show such indifference.

Thus exhorted by these songs of reality (*tattvagītikā*), the Blessed One—like one awakening from sleep—should manifest himself as the Blessed Śrī Hevajra, who has entered into union with Nairātmyā, arising from the syllable *aṃ* produced from the syllable *hūṃ* at the center of a sun-maṇḍala; having transformed all this into a single entity, [he visualizes] the form of the moon consisting of the essence of that nectar-fluid, above which are two seed-syllables, above which are two symbols produced from those two seeds, and above those, the two seed-syllables *hūṃ* and *oṃ*. Then, having merged all this into one, he should generate himself as the Blessed Śrī Hevajra, arisen from the syllable *aṃ* produced from the syllable *hūṃ* within the solar disc, in union with Nairātmyā.

One should meditate on [the deity] who is black in color, extremely fierce, with three eyes and tawny hair blazing upward from his head, which is marked by a double vajra (*viśvavajra*). His forehead is adorned above with a garland of five severed heads. He is terrifying with a frown and a knitting of the brows. His first face is black, the right white, and the left red; furthermore, the two faces to the left are black, as are the two faces to the right, while the upper face is smoke-colored. All the faces are distorted, formidable with bared fangs, and possess three eyes. In the eight lotus vessels held in his eight right hands, there are, in order: an elephant, horse, donkey, cow, camel, human, dog (*śarabha*), and buffalo. Likewise, in the eight skull-cups of his left hands are: Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Tejas (Fire), Candra (Moon), Āditya (Sun), Yama, and Dhanada (Kubera). His body is endowed with the six seals (*ṣanmudrā*) and adorned with a half-garland of heads. Naked, he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, treading upon the four Māras—Skandha, Kleśa, Mṛtyu, and Devaputra—and stands in a dancing pose upon a solar disc. [Near him is] Nairātmā, who is black, two-armed, and holds a flaying knife (*kartī*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*) in her right and left hands respectively, embracing the Blessed One. She is naked, endowed with the five seals, three-eyed, with tawny hair standing erect, and her head is adorned with a garland of heads and a garland of dried human skulls.
One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady, her limbs adorned, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, possessed of supreme great passion, and united in union with the Blessed One.

Thus, having clearly visualized the maṇḍala circle as it was seen—surrounded by the host of vidyās and filling the expanse of space with a mass of its own rays—one should emit rays from the seed-syllable situated in one’s own heart. These rays pervade the entire triple world and then cause [the deity] to enter back into that very syllable. Having again expanded [them] into the hollow of space, one should draw forth the wisdom-circle (jñānacakra) before oneself; having made it manifest and performed worship, one should bring it and cause it to enter one’s own pledge-circle (samayacakra). Having caused it to enter and become one, while maintaining the divine pride (*devatāhaṅkāra*), one should visualize oneself being consecrated by the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, vidyā-deities, and Lords of Wrath with vases filled with the five nectars, and being worshipped with various special offerings, by means of the mass of rays emerging from one’s own body.

Thus, in due order, without skipping the four moments characterized by variety (*vicitra*), ripening (*vipāka*), crushing (*vimarda*), and the signless (*vilakṣaṇa*), one should perceive the four joys—the joy of delight (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), and innate joy (*sahajānanda*)—and receive the four empowerments ending with the great bliss of the secret wisdom consort, through the four purities of laughing, gazing, embracing, and union. Once empowered, with one's head marked by the Lord of one's own family, one should seal Gaurī and the others with the Mind Lords Śāśvata, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Amitābha, and Pukkasī and the others with Hatred, Delusion, Jealousy, and Passion; thus one should mark [the deities] upon the head.

And this Blessed One possesses the wheel (*sacakra*) and consists of the five wisdoms. In that regard, the moon, which is the transformation of the vowel *a* (*āli*), has the nature of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). The sun, which is the transformation of the consonant *ka* (*kāli*), has the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). The seed-syllable of the emblem situated between them is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Their unification into one is the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). The perfection of the image is the wisdom of the utterly pure sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). Thus, one should cultivate the conviction that the entire triple world has the form of the maṇḍala-circle. And having seen that this has emerged from the bodhicitta born of the great bliss of the single flavor of wisdom and method, one should contemplate that the goddesses Gaurī and the others have entered sequentially into their own eight mouths. Having thus perceived the entire triple world as a single body consisting of wisdom and method, one should seal it with the four wheels according to their respective places. At the head is the wheel of great bliss, a lotus of thirty-two petals; thereupon, one should see the filaments and the brilliantly shining white syllable *haṃ*. At the throat is the enjoyment wheel, a sixteen-petaled lotus, in the center of which is the red syllable *oṃ*.

In the heart, at the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*), one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus with a blue syllable *HŪṂ* in its center. At the navel, at the wheel of emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*), one should meditate on a sixty-four-petaled lotus with the syllable *AṂ* in its core, emitting five-colored rays of light. Having clearly visualized these wheels, one should expand the mass of their rays into the sky and cause them to dissolve back into those very same wheels. Then, one should armor oneself with the Tathāgatas residing within one’s own body in the form of the six mudrās:
Akṣobhya in the form of a crown-ornament (*cakrin*), and Amitābha as the nature of the earrings (*kuṇḍala*).
Ratneśa resides in the necklace of the neck, and Vairocana is situated in the hand.
Amoghasiddhi resides in the girdle; Vajradhṛk dwells in all the limbs;
Mohavajrī should be in the two eyes, and Dveṣavajrī in the two ears.
In the nose she is known as Mātsaryavajrī, and in the mouth as Rāgavajrikā;
in touch she is Īrṣyāvajrī, and the mind is the Yoginī Nairātmā.
One should empower the body-awakening in the mind as the seed-syllable in the moon at the heart;
the mantra is *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*.
She is Khecarī, Bhūcarī, and likewise Pātālavāsinī.

Having thus become one who observes the pledge (*samayin*), one should recite the mantra according to this procedure: whichever syllables of the mantra are emitted, they emerge from the mouth of the deity with rays of light; these enter one’s own mouth, are emitted through the path of the *vajra*, and enter the lotus of the deity. Again, from the mouth of the deity they enter one’s own mouth. One should repeat the empowerment mantra (*adhiṣṭhāna-mantra*) in this sequence. However, in the case of different ritual actions (*karma*), a change in the color [of the syllables] must be performed.

Having thus recited the mantra to the limit of one's endurance without weariness, one should then meditate upon a blue syllable *HŪṂ* within the sun and moon at one’s own heart, its form vibrating and withdrawing. One should visualize the syllable *AṂ* within the moon at Nairātmyā’s heart. One should contemplate the Blessed Lady, having melted together with that very moon-maṇḍala of the syllable *AṂ*, entering into the heart of the Blessed Lord. Then the Blessed Lord also, having emanated a mass of light rays from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated within the sun and moon at his own heart—expanding them through the eight hundred breaths of the *Ālikāli* [mantra] and then withdrawing them—enters therein himself and becomes one.
And [the practitioner] is established within the seed-syllable in the center of the enclosure of the moon and sun. At this point, one should remember this:
"Neither beginning nor end, neither here nor there; neither existence nor nirvana.
This is that supreme great bliss—neither other nor self."

Thereupon, the seed-syllable, the moon, and the sun, having merged together, take on the nature of nectar in the form of a ray of light. One should meditate on this, gradually becoming unperceivable like the flame of a lamp, following the sequence of the four junctions (*catuḥsandhyā*) preceded by praise, worship, offerings, and oblations.
Oṃ inda jama jakkha bhūta vahni vāyu rakkha | canda sujja māda bappa talapātāle aṭṭhasappa svāhā ||
Consume this offering; smell the flowers, incense, meat, and liquor.
Accomplish all our purposes with water; grant us patience and remove our bonds.
Oṃ, the syllable *a* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen; Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā. This is the mantra for the bali offering to all spirits.

Oṃ, to the eight-faced one, whose tawny hair swirls upward, who has twenty-four eyes and sixteen arms, whose body is like a black cloud, who wears many garlands of skulls, whose mind is exceedingly fierce, and who has fangs like a half-moon.
Oṃ māraya 2 kāraya 2 garjaya 2 tarjaya 2 śoṣaya 2 saptasāgarān bandha 2 nāgāṣṭakān gṛhṇa 2 śatrūn ha hā hi hī hu hū he hai ho hau haṃ haḥ phaṭ svāhā. This is the root mantra of the Blessed One.
Oṃ deva picuvajra hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā. This is the heart mantra. Oṃ vajra karttari hevajrāya hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā. This is the near-heart mantra.
Oṃ a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa svāhā. This is the mantra for subduing the city.
At the time of offering the first worship and garland, one should recite this other supreme samaya-song: "The *bolā* resides at Kollaire; the *kakkolā* resides at Mummuṇire."
The clouds have become dense; alas, compassion is being shown, yet no *rolā* song is sung.
There fine wine is drunk and strong liquor is sipped;
O friend Kālindarī, there the drum is beaten with passion. There the four-fold sandalwood paste, kakkola, saffron, and camphor are applied.
There, heaps of garlands, firewood, and śāliñja plants were being eaten.
While swinging and playing with balls, no distinction between pure and impure is perceived;
having climbed onto the dry wood, there the very essence is realized.
On the path of the sandalwood and the kundu-fruit, the drum of realization is beaten.

Thus, at the time of the worship of the assembly presided over during the junctions (*sandhyā*), this song should be sung by the mantra-practitioner holding the vajra and bell in order to bring about the presence of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). Furthermore, according to the sequence as prescribed, one should meditate upon the Blessed One within the mandala-circle: two-armed and one-faced, with a vajra in the right hand and a skull-bowl (*kapāla*) and *khaṭvāṅga* staff in the left; standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, naked, and trampling upon a corpse.
Likewise, [one may meditate on him] with four arms, a vajra in the right hand and a skull-bowl in the left, while the remaining two arms embrace his own consort (*svābhavidyā*).

In the same way, he has six arms and three faces—the left red and the right white. In his left hands are a trident and a bell; in his right hands are a vajra and a flaying knife (*karttikā*). With his remaining two arms, he embraces his consort (*svābhavidyā*). And that Blessed Lady embraces the Blessed One with her two arms holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup (*kapāla*). These [forms] have two, four, or six arms. They are blue in color, three-eyed, with tawny hair standing erect, endowed with the six mudrās, naked, and should be visualized as standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, treading upon corpses. However, because of the absence of eight faces, one should cause the circle of goddesses (*devatīcakra*) to enter into one's own body.
Oṃ trailokyākṣepa hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā. This is the recitation mantra of the two-armed [form]. Oṃ jvala 2 jvalabhyaḥ hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā. This is the recitation mantra of the four-armed [form].
Oṃ kiṭi 2 vajra hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā. This is the recitation mantra of the six-armed [form].

The remainder should be performed according to the previous procedure. It should be done in another way as follows: out of compassion, he has red eyes; out of a mind of loving-kindness, his body is black; and by means of the four bases of sympathetic appeal, his four feet are remembered [as being marked with wheels].
He has eight faces, the eight liberations, sixteen arms, and the sixteen emptinesses;
his limbs bear the five mudrās, and he is wrathful for the sake of subduing the wicked.
Pukkasi is known by the flesh, Śavarī is conceived through the blood;
Caṇḍālī is in the form of semen, and Ḍombinī is in the marrow and fat.

Having resolved that the skin is the seven factors of enlightenment and the bones are the four truths, the practitioner should dwell in the yoga of the deity and make the aspiration: "Born of noble family, free from madness, observing the commitments, may I be a teacher of Hevajra."
May I be compassionate and devoted to my guru in birth after birth.
"May I, with hands ringing the vajra and bell, reciting the profound Dharma, and gathering the semen of women, exist in birth after birth. Thus [it is said].
This has been written by me, of dull intellect, through the force of faith; whatever herein may be flawed should be corrected by those who know the truth, and my virtuous friends should forgive me.

Out of compassion for sentient beings and through devotion to the lotus feet of his guru, [the author] was the son of the ornament of the Lunar dynasty; by him, having obtained the necessary means, and having composed this difficult-to-attain manual of practice (*sādhanopāyikā*) for the illustrious Hevajra, I have conquered the enemies who take pride in their own status.
"By whatever merit has been accumulated by me, may the world become a holder of the vajra. Thus.
The *Śrīhevajrasādhanopāyikā* is completed.
